mass-spectra-s1.title: Mass spectrum of a pure element
mass-spectra-s1.text: A sample of a pure element is turned into singly charged positive ions (each atom loses one electron) and passed through a mass spectrometer. The isotope masses are 23.985, 24.986 and 25.983 amu.

mass-spectra-s2.title: Isotopes of three elements
mass-spectra-s2.text: The table lists isotope masses and natural abundances.

items.q: What do all atoms of one element have in common?
options: The same number of neutrons
The same mass number
The same number of protons
The same mass, to the nearest 0.001 amu

why.correct: The atomic number (number of protons) identifies the element. Neutrons, and so mass, can vary.
options: Atoms of one element can differ in neutrons; those are isotopes.
Isotopes of one element have different mass numbers.
Right: the number of protons, the atomic number, defines the element.
Different isotopes have different masses.

items.q: An atom of chlorine has 17 protons and 20 neutrons. What is its mass number?

why.correct: Mass number = protons + neutrons = 37. This atom is chlorine-37, written ³⁷Cl.
options: Right: mass number = protons + neutrons = 17 + 20.
That is the atomic number, the protons alone.
That is the number of neutrons alone.
Subtracting gives no standard quantity; the mass number adds the two.

items.q: How many neutrons are in an atom of iron-56? Iron has atomic number 26.

mistakes.why: Value: you added the numbers. The mass number already includes the protons, so subtract: 56 − 26.

items.q: How many isotopes of this element does the spectrum show?
options: One, since the sample is a pure element
Three
Twenty-five, the middle mass
Two, since the smaller peaks count as one

why.correct: One peak per isotope: three peaks, three isotopes, with mass numbers 24, 25 and 26.
options: A pure element can still be a mix of isotopes; each peak is one.
Right: each peak is ions of one isotope, and there are three peaks.
The m/z values are masses, not a count of isotopes.
The peaks at 25 and 26 have different masses, so they are different isotopes.

items.q: Calculate the average atomic mass of the element from the spectrum.

mistakes.why: Value: you took a simple average of the three masses. Weight each mass by its abundance: most atoms are the light isotope.
Value: you used percents, not fractions. Divide each abundance by 100 (78.99% is 0.7899).

items.q: Which element is this, and what evidence supports the claim?
options: Sodium, because the tallest peak is near 23
Chromium, because three isotopes add to a mass near 75
Aluminum, because 24 + 25 + 26 is close to 27 times 3
Magnesium, whose atomic mass on the periodic table is 24.31

why.correct: The abundance-weighted average, 24.31 amu, is the atomic mass of magnesium. An element is identified by matching its average atomic mass (and, with more data, its atomic number).
options: The tallest peak is at 24, and sodium's average is 22.99, which does not match 24.31.
Atomic mass is a weighted average of the isotopes, not their sum.
A simple average of the mass numbers is 25, and aluminum's is 26.98: neither matches.
Right: the weighted average, 24.31 amu, matches magnesium.

items.q: Why is the average atomic mass much closer to 24 than to 25?
options: About 79% of the atoms are the isotope of mass 24
The isotope of mass 24 has the most protons
Heavier isotopes are not counted in the average
The spectrometer detects lighter ions more easily

why.correct: A weighted average sits nearest the most abundant isotope. Here 78.99% of the atoms have mass about 24.
options: Right: the most abundant isotope pulls the weighted average toward its mass.
Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons.
All isotopes count, each weighted by its abundance.
The peak heights reflect how many atoms of each isotope are present, not a detector bias.

items.q: How do the atoms that make the peak at m/z = 26 differ from those at m/z = 24?
options: They have two more protons
They have two more electrons
They have two more neutrons
They carry a charge of 2+ instead of 1+

why.correct: Isotopes differ only in neutrons. Mass 26 vs 24: two extra neutrons, same 12 protons.
options: Two more protons would make a different element.
Electrons barely change the mass, and every ion here has lost one electron.
Right: same element (same protons), mass two units higher, so two more neutrons.
Every ion in this spectrum is singly charged, so m/z equals the mass.

items.q: Calculate the average atomic mass of gallium from the table.

mistakes.why: Value: that is a simple average. Gallium-69 is more common, so weight each mass by its abundance.

items.q: Boron's average atomic mass is 10.81 amu. Using the table, what percentage of boron atoms are boron-11?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the boron-10 share. The average (10.81) is closer to 11, so most atoms are boron-11.

why.correct: Let x be the fraction of ¹¹B. 10.013(1 − x) + 11.009x = 10.81, so 0.996x = 0.797 and x = 0.800, or 80.0%.

items.q: A student says chlorine's mass spectrum would show one peak at 35.45, the atomic mass on the periodic table. Which response is correct?
options: Yes, because the spectrometer reports the average mass of the atoms in the sample
No; the spectrum shows peaks at 35 and 37 of equal height
No; it shows one peak at 36, halfway between the isotopes
No; it shows peaks near 35 and 37, the first about three times taller

why.correct: The periodic-table value is a weighted average of real isotopes. The spectrum shows each isotope: a tall peak at 35 and one about a third as tall at 37.
options: A mass spectrometer separates the isotopes and shows each one as a peak.
The heights follow the abundances, 75.76% and 24.24%, about 3 to 1.
No chlorine atom has mass 36 in this data; the peaks are at each isotope's mass.
Right: 35.45 is an average. Each peak is a real isotope, and the heights follow 75.76% and 24.24%.

items.q: Gallium's average atomic mass, 69.72 amu, falls between its two isotope masses. Which claim about the data is supported?
options: A third gallium isotope with a mass near 69.7 is likely
The average is nearer 69 because gallium-69 is the more common isotope
Gallium-71 has more protons than gallium-69
The abundances are probably wrong, since the mass is below the midpoint

why.correct: The midpoint of 68.926 and 70.925 is 69.93. The real average, 69.72, sits closer to 69 because the lighter isotope is the majority.
options: A weighted average of two isotopes always falls between them; no third isotope is needed.
Right: 60.11% of atoms are gallium-69, which pulls the average below the midpoint of 69.93.
Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons; gallium-71 has two more neutrons.
An average below the midpoint is what you expect when the lighter isotope is more common.

items.q: An atom of oxygen gains two electrons. What does it become?
options: A cation with a 2+ charge
An anion with a 2− charge
An isotope of oxygen with a mass two units higher
An atom of neon, which has two more electrons

why.correct: O has 8 protons. With 10 electrons the charge is 8 − 10 = 2−: the oxide anion, O²⁻.
options: Gaining electrons adds negative charge; a cation forms when electrons are lost.
Right: two extra electrons give two more negative charges than positive ones.
Electrons barely change the mass, and isotopes differ in neutrons, not electrons.
The element depends on protons; oxygen keeps its 8 protons.

items.q: Which particles have more protons than electrons? Select all that apply.
options: Na⁺
Cl⁻
O²⁻
Ne

why.correct: A cation (positive ion) has more protons than electrons. Na⁺ is the only cation here; Cl⁻ and O²⁻ are anions and Ne is neutral.
options: Right: 11 protons, 10 electrons.
Chloride has 17 protons and 18 electrons: more electrons.
Oxide has 8 protons and 10 electrons: more electrons.
A neutral atom has equal numbers: 10 and 10.

items.q: In a mass spectrometer, why are the atoms first turned into ions?
options: The fields that steer and sort particles act on charged particles
Removing an electron makes each atom lighter, so the peaks spread out
Ions of different isotopes differ in protons, which the detector counts
Neutral atoms of one element share one mass, so they need no sorting

why.correct: The spectrometer sorts particles by mass using fields that act only on charge. For the singly charged ions in this course, m/z equals the mass.
options: Right: the fields push on charged particles; a neutral atom would fly straight through unsorted.
An electron is about 1/1800 of a proton's mass, so removing one barely changes the mass.
Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons.
Neutral atoms of one element can still differ in mass; they just cannot be steered.

items.q: Which pair are isotopes of each other?
options: ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca
¹⁶O and ¹⁶O²⁻
²⁸Si and ³⁰Si
¹²C and ¹⁴N

why.correct: Isotopes: same element (same atomic number), different mass numbers.
options: Same mass number but different elements (18 and 20 protons).
Same isotope; one has gained electrons to become an ion.
Right: both are silicon (14 protons) with different neutron counts.
Different elements, with 6 and 7 protons.
